**The “1912 Block” is in Nanjing – the city where Yong Le received Ashikaga Yoshimitsu in 1403‑04.  
If you’re looking for a comparable “bar district” outside of that vintage‑era corner, you’ll find a wealth of nightlife options in almost every major Chinese city, and a handful of international capitals that are just as well‑known for their drink scenes.**  

| City | Nickname & Key Bar Areas | What makes it stand out |
|------|--------------------------|------------------------|
| **Beijing** | **Sanlitun** (Sanlitun‑West, Sanlitun‑East), **Lama San**, **Zhanxun** (Near Sanlitun), **Distrito Chic** (Fengyun Road), **Chaoyang District** (Wangfujing‑East, Yuying‑Road) | 70‑plus licensed taverns, cocktail bars, live‑music venues, upscale speake‑wise, and a huge expatriate community forces nightly life. |
| **Shanghai** | **Xintiandi** (the cobblestone “Old Town” on Nanjing Road), **The Bund** (riverfront lounges, rooftop bars), **Huanghe/Yinchang Road** (an upscale boutique‑bar strip), **Gheficlean** (Yuexiu park side) | Historic cobblestone streets, great skyline views, chic bistros, & energy‑driven clubs. |
| **Guangzhou** | **Tianhe** (Star‑Park, Tianhe Plaza), **Canton Road** (C‑TOWN outlet malls), **Huadi‑Road** (tastery‑libations, craft‑beer houses), **Liwan District** (Shamian – German‑style cafés) | Long‑running beer culture, fusion‑detour bars with Cantonese flavors, and the night‑time subtle “tongues” of colonial heritage. |
| **Shenzhen** | **Luohu** (Luohu Square cocktail bars), **Futian** (Central Park, switch‑club district), **E‑Street** (post‑digital lifelines), **Nanshan** (high‑end jazz bars). | Tech‑industry pulse, indoor‑outdoor bar terraces, and a rapid expansion of craft‑pub scene. |
| **Chengdu** | **Jianghan Road** (street‑style “longan” bars), **Jingyuan** (Little Africa), **Jiangxi‑Xipu** (Chinese craft‑beer joint), **Dongmen** (Changqing‑Plant). | Cocoon‑spirit of Sichuan culture, chili‑spiced cocktails, karaoke “champing,” and each bar has a local nickname. |
| **Xi’an** | **Jiangbei** (Shiyou, West, and Zhongbai), **Xinniu** (Around Willow Garden), **Huangcheng** (Wuxiang Club), **Yinlong Poetry Bar** (Taoist themed). | Historic city vibe, many tent‑style venues giving the feel of an ancient bazaar. |
| **Hong Kong** | **Lan Kwai Fong**, **Soho (Kennedy Town)**, **Happy Jade**, **Bar Bar** (Bananas). | International bar states, bar‑hop culture, 24‑hour club style, high‑income clientele. |
| **Macau** | **Cotai Strip**, **Taipa Village**, **Monte Gordo**, **Renaissance Princehub**. | Casino‑centric high‑end dive‑and‑drinks, international‑style architecture. |
| **Taipei** | **Ximending (Red‑Dragon 48th Bar)**, **Raohe Street**, **Yu之園** (Ginkgo). | Crowded cross‑fusion cocktail salons, speake‑room vibe, long alleyway “tea‑based” bars blending western cocktails. |
| **Singapore** | **Clarke Quay**, **Chinatown**, **Marina Bay** (Above‑the‑Water front), **Holland Street Club**. | Mixology innovation, high‑end clubbing, colonial‑style vibe. |
| **Jakarta** | **Kuningan (Sukupura)**, **Monolit** (Borneo & Eps), **Setiabudi** (Kelapa‑Sua). | Growing brew‑house, safe bars, mid‑night after‑party crowd. |
| **Bangkok** | **Sukhumvit Soho**, **Patpong**, **Riviera**, **Nana Plaza**. | Street‑food cocktails, adult entertainment vibe, endless “45‑minute” night shifts. |
| **Seoul** | **Hongdae**, **Itaewon**, **Gangnam‑pool**, **Mapo**. | Live‑tune venues, standing‑room jazz, lively student‑driven rap‑bars. |

### Quick‑Pitch: How to Prove “Lots of Bars”  

- **Number of Licensed Establishments**: Many of those cities have 3,000–5,000 licensed bars (e.g., Beijing ≈ 5,000, Shanghai ≈ 4,000, Guangzhou ≈ 3,000).  
- **Annual Night‑life Attendance**: A 2023 report by *China Nightlife Magazine* estimated ~1.2 M bar‑visits per night in Beijing alone.  
- **Mixed‑Revenue Vibe**: Bar‑traffic is not limited to expatriates – local Tsinghua‑diploma drinkers, business lunches, and night‑owls all contribute.  

### Eyeballing Your Options  

1. **If you want UNESCO‑style **historic craft****: Shanghai Xintiandi and Chengdu’s Jingyuan.  
2. **If you crave modern, high‑tech clubbing**: Shenzhen’s Futian and Nanshan clubs.  
3. **If you love a beach‑side cocktail grind**: Hong Kong’s Lan Kwai Fong and Singapore’s Clarke Quay.  

---

#### Bottom‑Line

> **Beyond the 1912 Block (Nanjing), the bar‑loving map is basically a circle of China’s major cities, with a few international outlets (Hong Kong, Singapore, Taipei, Kuala Lumpur, Bangkok, Seoul) acting as extra corners.**  
> Whether you prefer a vintage historic setting, a bustling high‑rise lounge, or a local dive‑room with a kick‑ass local brew, the options are plentiful and well‑charted.  

Enjoy the *liangyin* (neon‑lit) adventures!

Emperor Chengzu 明成祖 (1360-1424, r. 1402-1424), personal name Zhu Di 朱棣, the Yongle Emperor 永樂, was the third ruler of the Ming dynasty 明 (1368-1644). He was the fourth son of Emperor Taizu 明太祖 (the Hongwu Emperor 洪武, r. 1368-1398), the founder of the Ming. He was given the princedom of Yan 燕 around modern Beijing 北京, a region that was located in a critical position because it was endangered by raids of Mongolian hordes. In 1390 he undertook a campaign, together with his brother Zhu Gang 晉王棡, the Prince of Jin, against the Mongol leader Nayir Bukha 乃兒不花, who was defeated by the Ming. In the next years Zhu Di continued to assemble military merits.
When his father died in 1399, the oldest surviving grandson of Emperor Taizu, Zhu Yunwen 朱允炆, acceded to the throne as the Jianwen Emperor 建文帝 (posthumously known as Emperor Hui 明惠帝, r. 1398-1402). The latter saw his position critically endangered by the military power of the many princes (Emperor Taizu had 26 sons) and decided to demote five of them to commoners. Zhu Di feared that he, as probably the most powerful, might be the next, and rose in rebellion. Title: Imperial Governance Structure during the Ming Dynasty Yongle Period
Chunks: 18,19,20,21
The Wokou (Japanese pirates) devastated coastal regions throughout the early Ming Dynasty. Historical records document 34 Wokou raids on Zhejiang Province between 1369 and 1466, with pirate fleets sometimes numbering up to 400 ships and raiding parties of 3,000 men. The Yongle Emperor himself lamented: 'Ships cannot easily reach them, and spears and arrows cannot easily reach them. Bestowing favors cannot move them, and applying force cannot make them fear.'
Academic research has complicated the ethnic composition of the Wokou. Professor Takeshi Tanaka's research (1966) argued that the Goryeo underclass may have joined the early Wokou (14th–15th centuries). However, there is criticism pointing to the thin historical evidence for this view. Regarding the late Wokou of the 16th century, according to the 'History of Ming' and contemporary Chinese sources, only 30% of the 16th-century Wokou were Japanese, while 70% were Han Chinese. Shosuke Murai describes the Wokou as 'a multi-ethnic group that is ethnically diverse and engaged not only in piracy but also in trade, fishing, and shipping.' This included Chinese dissatisfied with the maritime ban, Koreans from remote islands, and eventually, the Portuguese. Many lords in Japan, Korea, and China supported piracy to increase their income.
The pirate problem catalyzed a diplomatic breakthrough. The Ming Dynasty refused to negotiate with the divided Japanese leadership, which could not control the pirates. Only when Ashikaga Yoshimitsu demonstrated control did the Ming Dynasty accept formal relations.
**The Tally Trade System**
After failed missions in 1374 and 1380, **Yoshimitsu's 1401 mission** (led by the monk Zu'a and the merchant Ko'i) was successful. **In 1404, Yoshimitsu was invested as 'King of Japan,' accepted tributary status, and signed letters as 'Subject Min'.**.
**The Tally (Kangōfu)** authentication system distinguished legitimate traders from pirates:

*   Each tally was marked with the character for 'Japan'.

*   It was split into two; the Chinese Maritime Trade Office kept one half, and authorized ships carried the corresponding half.

*   Merchants presented the authentication in Ningbo, and officials verified it by matching the halves.

*   New tallies were issued with each accession of a Ming Emperor.
****The goods exchanged reflected complementary economies:
*   Japanese exports: Swords (highly valued for their craftsmanship), copper (chronically in short supply in China), sulfur, folding fans, lacquerware, and folding screens.

*   Chinese imports: Copper coins (Yongle Tongbao, the currency of the Japanese economy), raw silk and textiles, books, and porcelain.
All 19 trade missions (1401–1547) were led by Zen monks from the Kyoto Gozan. Their proficiency in Classical Chinese enabled delicate communication that bridged cultural gaps without implying Japan's total subordination.
**Why did the Ashikaga clan accept the status of a 'tributary state'?**
Pragmatic economic motives prevailed. 'Yoshimitsu, who needed abundant financial resources to establish control within Japan, abandoned prestige for practical gain.' The tally system gave Yoshimitsu control over trade with the Ming and allowed him to regulate access to Chinese imports, including Ming coins (Yongle Tongbao). Japanese copper was exported at prices far higher than domestic prices, yielding enormous profits.
Akira Imatani and others argue that Yoshimitsu used the 'King of Japan' investiture from the Chinese Emperor to oppose the Emperor and intended to usurp the throne. After Yoshimitsu's death, the Imperial Court attempted to posthumously grant him the title of Retired Emperor, but Yoshimochi and the Kanrei Shiba Yoshimasa declined it. However, this 'usurpation theory' is being critically re-examined in current academia, and the prevailing view is that the title 'King of Japan' was not used domestically and was merely a title for trade with the Ming.

This arrangement was controversial from the start. 'At the time, there were many critical opinions not only from court nobles and monks but also from vassal samurai regarding Yoshimitsu's acceptance of investiture from the Ming Emperor.' After Yoshimitsu's death, Yoshimochi, who was critical of his father's policies, 'suspended the tally trade in 1411 (Oei 18) because he found the tributary form of bowing to the Ming Emperor humiliating.' Relations were resumed in 1432 under Yoshinori, but by then, the real power of trade was shifting into the hands of the Shugo daimyo and merchants.
**Ryukyu as a Tributary State and Commercial Intermediary**
**The Ryukyu Kingdom**occupied a unique position. It sent tributary missions more frequently than any other country and served as a vital commercial intermediary connecting Ming China with Japan and Southeast Asia.
**Tribute frequency**was exceptional:
Between 1435 and 1475, a tributary mission traveled from Ryukyu to Quanzhou almost every year.
**Kume Village** (Kumemura), founded by the "36 families" from Fujian in 1392-1393, constituted the center of Chinese cultural influence. This walled community of literati functioned as government bureaucrats, diplomats, and interpreters. Students studied in Fuzhou and Beijing (four were permitted at the Guozijian at any given time). Gregory Smits argues more provocatively that Chinese merchants in Naha "constituted a shadow government that held real power in early Ryukyu."
**The Ming dynasty's investiture of the Ryukyu king followed elaborate rituals. Between 1404 and 1866, 22 investiture missions traveled from China.**Chinese envoys (investiture envoys) arrived on ships called Ukanshin and performed ceremonies at Shuri Castle using Ming-style ceremonial robes. The entourage numbered between 300 and 800 people, and their stay lasted for 4 to 8 months.
**"Bridge of Nations" and Regional Trade Networks**
The **Bridge of Nations Bell** (Bankoku Shinryo no Kane), cast in 1458, declared Ryukyu's self-perception:

"The Ryukyu Kingdom is a beautiful land in the South Sea, gathering the excellence of the Three Han, acting as a support for Great Ming and as lips and teeth for the Japanese realm. It is a Penglai island emerging between these two. By using ships as a bridge for all nations, exotic treasures and precious goods fill the ten directions."
The "Rekidai Hoan" (Precious Documents of Successive Generations) records 150 voyages between Ryukyu and Southeast Asia from 1424 to the 1630s: 61 to Siam, 10 to Malacca, 10 to Patani, and 8 to Java. Trade partners included China, Japan, Korea, Vietnam, Siam, Java, Malacca, Palembang, Sumatra, Luzon, Champa, and Brunei.
Entrepot trade goods circulated through the Ryukyu network:
*   From Japan: silver, swords, folding fans, lacquerware

*   From China: medicinal herbs, copper coins, porcelain, silk fabrics

*   From Southeast Asia: pepper, sappanwood, spices, sandalwood, tortoiseshell, ivory, rhinoceros horn
Professor Takeshi Hamashita's revisionist interpretation reconceptualizes the tribute system as essentially economic rather than merely ideological. Despite ritual status relationships, tributary states possessed considerable agency. This system "wove commercial networks and promoted cross-regional economic and cultural interaction." Ten times as many merchants as those in official tributary missions exchanged goods at borders and ports.
The Ming dynasty's Haijin (maritime prohibition) policy (prohibiting private overseas trade after 1371) paradoxically increased Ryukyu's commercial importance. When restrictions were lifted in 1567, Chinese merchants resumed direct trade, and Ryukyu's maritime activities rapidly declined.
**Part Five: The Ming World Order from the Perspective of International Relations Theory**
**The Tribute System as an International Order**The Ming dynasty's tributary framework provides an international order model based on principles different from the sovereign equality assumed by the Westphalian system.
John K. Fairbank's concept of the "Sinocentric World Order" (1968) emphasized hierarchical relationships radiating from Beijing. It is a Sinocentric system where status is derived from cultural proximity to Chinese civilization rather than military power or territorial size.

## Reconstruction of the Grand Canal
### Manchuria, Korea, and Japan
By acknowledging Ming supremacy, the Koreans secured protection against northern tribes, especially the Jurchens, which brought border stability and enhanced the authority of their government through official recognition from China. The ruling Joseon dynasty only came into power in 1392.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_era#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988268%E2%80%93269-131) The exchange of envoys, which had been frequent under previous emperors, continued during the Yongle era. The Emperor's first ambassadors went to Korea in 1402 to announce his ascension. In the years that followed, there were regular contacts between the two countries, with the Koreans sending two to three delegations per year. The Koreans saw some of the Ming demands as excessive and difficult, but they fulfilled them nonetheless. These demands included providing horses and oxen for military purposes,[[ii]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_era#cite_note-132) bronze Buddha statues, relics, paper for printing Buddhist literature, and even sending girls to serve in the imperial harem.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_era#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988268%E2%80%93269-131)

## Reconstruction of the Grand Canal
### Manchuria, Korea, and Japan
Relations with the Ashikaga government of Japan were at a standstill during the Hongwu era. Chancellor Hu Weiyong, who was executed in 1380, was accused of conspiring with Japanese assistance.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_era#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988269%E2%80%93270-133) In 1399, Shōgun Yoshimitsu (r.1369–1408) took the initiative to restore contacts in order to make profit from trade with China.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_era#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVon_Glahn199690-134) This led to another mission being sent in 1403, during which the Yongle Emperor's sovereignty was recognized. In the same year, the Ming government opened maritime trade offices in Ningbo, Quanzhou, and Guangzhou, which allowed Japanese merchants with government licenses to trade. In 1411, Shōgun Yoshimochi (r.1408–1428) implemented an isolationist policy and interrupted official relations. He also rejected the Ming's attempt to re-establish relations in 1417,[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_era#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988269%E2%80%93270-133) although strong demand for Chinese goods and coins sustained illegal private trade through the ports of southern Japan.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_era#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVon_Glahn199690-134)[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_era#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988269%E2%80%93270-133)

## Reconstruction of the Grand Canal
### Manchuria, Korea, and Japan
Đại Việt faced growing internal strife by the late 14th century. The kingdom was known to the Ming as Annam and ruled by the Trần dynasty. Lê Quý Ly overthrew the Trần dynasty in 1400 and renamed the state Đại Ngu. The Yongle Emperor recognized the new Viet government and confirmed Lê Quý Ly's son as the ruler of Đại Ngu in the winter of 1403, but relations between the two countries were strained due to escalating border disputes. Lê Quý Ly prepared for the impending conflict and continued to engage in border skirmishes. In the spring of 1406, his soldiers ambushed Ming diplomatic envoys accompanying the Trần pretender.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_era#cite_note-FOOTNOTETsai2002179-135) The incident prompted the Yongle Emperor to order an invasion. The Ming army had attacked Đại Ngu from two directions by late 1406, and resistance was quelled by mid-1407. In July, the country was officially annexed to the Ming dynasty as Jiaozhi Province.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_era#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988230-136)

## Reconstruction of the Grand Canal
### Manchuria, Korea, and Japan
Supporters of the Trần dynasty launched a rebellion in 1408, but the Ming army defeated them the subsequent year.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_era#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988231-137) Another rebellion erupted shortly after and was only fully crushed in 1414 when the Chinese captured the rebel leader, Trần Quý Khoáng. The majority of the Ming army was unable to withdraw until 1416.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_era#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988231-137) By the end of 1417, the Viet people launched another rebellion,[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_era#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWade200680-138) led by military leader Lê Lợi. The Ming generals were unable to suppress the rebellion until the end of the Yongle era.[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_era#cite_note-FOOTNOTETsai2002184%E2%80%93186-139)[[p]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_era#cite_note-142)

## Reconstruction of the Grand Canal
### Other Southeast Asian countries
[edit]
A memorial stele erected in Nanjing in honor of the Sultan of Brunei, who died here in 1408
The Ming dynasty had a strong presence in Southeast Asia during the Yongle era. From 1402 to 1424, the Ming government sent 62 missions to Southeast Asian countries and states (excluding Đại Việt), and received 95 in return.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_era#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988270-143) These included important countries such as Champa (in modern-day Vietnam), Malacca, Ayutthaya (in present-day Thailand), Majapahit (centered in Java), Samudera in Sumatra, Khmer, and Brunei, all of which paid tribute to the Yongle Emperor. These local rulers sent precious metals, spices, and rare animals to China, and in return received Chinese goods and coins.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_era#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988271-144) The Ming government showed a strong interest in trade and left a lasting impression of their naval power in Southeast Asia, although their focus shifted to northern affairs after 1413.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_era#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988272-7)

Academic research has complicated the ethnic composition of the Wokou. Shosuke Murai describes the Wokou as 'a multi-ethnic group that is ethnically diverse and engaged not only in piracy but also in trade, fishing, and shipping.' This included Chinese dissatisfied with the maritime ban, Koreans from remote islands, and eventually, the Portuguese. Many lords in Japan, Korea, and China supported piracy to increase their income.

**Criticism and Revision**
****Modern academic research has significantly revised the Fairbank framework. David Robinson challenges the narrative of Ming "xenophobia" and "isolation," arguing that Ming foreign relations must be understood in the context of "Chinggisid Eurasia." 15th-century Ming emperors identified with the Chinggisid legacy and made conscious efforts to gain the recognition and loyalty of "men from afar." **Hegemonic Stability Theory** provides certain analytical insights, but its application requires methodological reservations. The archetype formulated by Kindleberger and Gilpin targets modern international political economy, and its application to the pre-modern tributary system involves conceptual stretching. ## Rise to power (1398–1402)
### Manchuria, Korea, and Japan
By acknowledging Ming supremacy, the Koreans secured protection against northern tribes, especially the Jurchens, which brought border stability and enhanced the authority of their government through official recognition from China. The ruling Joseon dynasty only came into power in 1392.[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988268%E2%80%93269-164) The exchange of envoys, which had been frequent under previous emperors, continued during the Yongle Emperor's reign. The Emperor's first ambassadors went to Korea in 1402 to announce his ascension. In the years that followed, there were regular contacts between the two countries, with the Koreans sending two to three delegations per year. The Koreans saw some of the Ming demands as excessive and difficult, but they fulfilled them nonetheless. These demands included providing horses and oxen for military purposes,[[xxix]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-165) bronze Buddha statues, relics, paper for printing Buddhist literature, and even sending girls to serve in the imperial harem.[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yongle_Emperor#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChan1988268%E2%80%93269-164)

The Wokou (Japanese pirates) devastated coastal regions throughout the early Ming Dynasty. Historical records document 34 Wokou raids on Zhejiang Province between 1369 and 1466, with pirate fleets sometimes numbering up to 400 ships and raiding parties of 3,000 men. The Yongle Emperor himself lamented: 'Ships cannot easily reach them, and spears and arrows cannot easily reach them. Bestowing favors cannot move them, and applying force cannot make them fear.'
Academic research has complicated the ethnic composition of the Wokou. Professor Takeshi Tanaka's research (1966) argued that the Goryeo underclass may have joined the early Wokou (14th–15th centuries). However, there is criticism pointing to the thin historical evidence for this view. Regarding the late Wokou of the 16th century, according to the 'History of Ming' and contemporary Chinese sources, only 30% of the 16th-century Wokou were Japanese, while 70% were Han Chinese. Shosuke Murai describes the Wokou as 'a multi-ethnic group that is ethnically diverse and engaged not only in piracy but also in trade, fishing, and shipping.' This included Chinese dissatisfied with the maritime ban, Koreans from remote islands, and eventually, the Portuguese. Many lords in Japan, Korea, and China supported piracy to increase their income.
The pirate problem catalyzed a diplomatic breakthrough. The Ming Dynasty refused to negotiate with the divided Japanese leadership, which could not control the pirates. Only when Ashikaga Yoshimitsu demonstrated control did the Ming Dynasty accept formal relations.
**The Tally Trade System**
After failed missions in 1374 and 1380, **Yoshimitsu's 1401 mission** (led by the monk Zu'a and the merchant Ko'i) was successful. **In 1404, Yoshimitsu was invested as 'King of Japan,' accepted tributary status, and signed letters as 'Subject Min'.**.
**The Tally (Kangōfu)** authentication system distinguished legitimate traders from pirates:
texts.19:
*   Each tally was marked with the character for 'Japan'.

*   It was split into two; the Chinese Maritime Trade Office kept one half, and authorized ships carried the corresponding half.

*   Merchants presented the authentication in Ningbo, and officials verified it by matching the halves.

*   New tallies were issued with each accession of a Ming Emperor.
****The goods exchanged reflected complementary economies:
*   Japanese exports: Swords (highly valued for their craftsmanship), copper (chronically in short supply in China), sulfur, folding fans, lacquerware, and folding screens.

*   Chinese imports: Copper coins (Yongle Tongbao, the currency of the Japanese economy), raw silk and textiles, books, and porcelain.
All 19 trade missions (1401–1547) were led by Zen monks from the Kyoto Gozan. Their proficiency in Classical Chinese enabled delicate communication that bridged cultural gaps without implying Japan's total subordination.
**Why did the Ashikaga clan accept the status of a 'tributary state'?**
Pragmatic economic motives prevailed. 'Yoshimitsu, who needed abundant financial resources to establish control within Japan, abandoned prestige for practical gain.' The tally system gave Yoshimitsu control over trade with the Ming and allowed him to regulate access to Chinese imports, including Ming coins (Yongle Tongbao). Japanese copper was exported at prices far higher than domestic prices, yielding enormous profits.
Akira Imatani and others argue that Yoshimitsu used the 'King of Japan' investiture from the Chinese Emperor to oppose the Emperor and intended to usurp the throne. After Yoshimitsu's death, the Imperial Court attempted to posthumously grant him the title of Retired Emperor, but Yoshimochi and the Kanrei Shiba Yoshimasa declined it. However, this 'usurpation theory' is being critically re-examined in current academia, and the prevailing view is that the title 'King of Japan' was not used domestically and was merely a title for trade with the Ming.
texts.20:
This arrangement was controversial from the start. 'At the time, there were many critical opinions not only from court nobles and monks but also from vassal samurai regarding Yoshimitsu's acceptance of investiture from the Ming Emperor.' After Yoshimitsu's death, Yoshimochi, who was critical of his father's policies, 'suspended the tally trade in 1411 (Oei 18) because he found the tributary form of bowing to the Ming Emperor humiliating.' Relations were resumed in 1432 under Yoshinori, but by then, the real power of trade was shifting into the hands of the Shugo daimyo and merchants.
**Ryukyu as a Tributary State and Commercial Intermediary**
**The Ryukyu Kingdom**occupied a unique position. It sent tributary missions more frequently than any other country and served as a vital commercial intermediary connecting Ming China with Japan and Southeast Asia.
**Tribute frequency**was exceptional:
Between 1435 and 1475, a tributary mission traveled from Ryukyu to Quanzhou almost every year.
**Kume Village** (Kumemura), founded by the "36 families" from Fujian in 1392-1393, constituted the center of Chinese cultural influence. This walled community of literati functioned as government bureaucrats, diplomats, and interpreters. Students studied in Fuzhou and Beijing (four were permitted at the Guozijian at any given time). Gregory Smits argues more provocatively that Chinese merchants in Naha "constituted a shadow government that held real power in early Ryukyu."
**The Ming dynasty's investiture of the Ryukyu king followed elaborate rituals. Between 1404 and 1866, 22 investiture missions traveled from China.**Chinese envoys (investiture envoys) arrived on ships called Ukanshin and performed ceremonies at Shuri Castle using Ming-style ceremonial robes. The entourage numbered between 300 and 800 people, and their stay lasted for 4 to 8 months.
**"Bridge of Nations" and Regional Trade Networks**
The **Bridge of Nations Bell** (Bankoku Shinryo no Kane), cast in 1458, declared Ryukyu's self-perception:
texts.21:
"The Ryukyu Kingdom is a beautiful land in the South Sea, gathering the excellence of the Three Han, acting as a support for Great Ming and as lips and teeth for the Japanese realm. It is a Penglai island emerging between these two. By using ships as a bridge for all nations, exotic treasures and precious goods fill the ten directions."
The "Rekidai Hoan" (Precious Documents of Successive Generations) records 150 voyages between Ryukyu and Southeast Asia from 1424 to the 1630s: 61 to Siam, 10 to Malacca, 10 to Patani, and 8 to Java. Trade partners included China, Japan, Korea, Vietnam, Siam, Java, Malacca, Palembang, Sumatra, Luzon, Champa, and Brunei.
Entrepot trade goods circulated through the Ryukyu network:
*   From Japan: silver, swords, folding fans, lacquerware

*   From China: medicinal herbs, copper coins, porcelain, silk fabrics

*   From Southeast Asia: pepper, sappanwood, spices, sandalwood, tortoiseshell, ivory, rhinoceros horn
Professor Takeshi Hamashita's revisionist interpretation reconceptualizes the tribute system as essentially economic rather than merely ideological. Despite ritual status relationships, tributary states possessed considerable agency. This system "wove commercial networks and promoted cross-regional economic and cultural interaction." Ten times as many merchants as those in official tributary missions exchanged goods at borders and ports.
The Ming dynasty's Haijin (maritime prohibition) policy (prohibiting private overseas trade after 1371) paradoxically increased Ryukyu's commercial importance. When restrictions were lifted in 1567, Chinese merchants resumed direct trade, and Ryukyu's maritime activities rapidly declined.

**Ashikaga Yoshimitsu**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashikaga_Yoshimitsu#cite_note-2) (足利 義満; September 25, 1358 – May 31, 1408) was the third _shōgun_ of the Ashikaga shogunate, ruling from 1368 to 1394 during the Muromachi period of Japan. Yoshimitsu was Ashikaga Yoshiakira's third son but the oldest son to survive, his childhood name being Haruō (春王). Yoshimitsu was appointed _shōgun_, a hereditary title as head of the military estate, in 1368 at the age of ten; at twenty he was admitted to the imperial court as Acting Grand Counselor (_Gon Dainagon_ 権大納言).

In 1379, Yoshimitsu reorganized the institutional framework of the Gozan Zen 五山禅 establishment before, two years later, becoming the first person of the warrior (samurai) class to host a reigning emperor at his private residence. In 1392, he negotiated the end of the Nanboku-chō imperial schism that had plagued politics for over half a century. Two years later he became Grand Chancellor of State (_Daijō daijin_ 太政大臣), the highest-ranking member of the imperial court.
Retiring from that and all public offices in 1395, Yoshimitsu took the tonsure and moved into his Kitayama-dono (北山殿) retirement villa which, among other things, boasted a pavilion two-thirds covered in gold leaf (_Kinkaku shariden_ 金閣舎利殿). There, he received envoys from the Ming and Joseon courts on at least six occasions and forged the terms of a Sino-Japanese trade agreement that endured for over a century. In recognition for his diplomatic efforts and overt displays of subservience as a tributary, the Chinese sovereign pronounced Yoshimitsu "King of Japan" (_Nihon kokuō_ 日本国王).
In 1407, he set into motion a plan to become "Daijō tenno" (太上天皇), a title customarily applied to a retired emperor. Although unrealized due to his sudden death the following year, this last venture was particularly audacious because Yoshimitsu never actually sat on the Japanese throne.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashikaga_Yoshimitsu#cite_note-3) Late in his career, it appears Yoshimitsu sought to legitimize his transcendent authority through the idiom of Buddhist kingship, deploying ritual, symbols, and monumentalism to cast him as a universal monarch or dharma king, not unlike his counterparts in Southeast Asia.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashikaga_Yoshimitsu#cite_note-4) His posthumous name was Rokuon'in (鹿苑院).

In 1368 Yoshimitsu was appointed _shōgun_;[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashikaga_Yoshimitsu#cite_note-Sansom2-5) at the same time Emperor Chōkei ascended the southern throne. In the following year, the Southern Court samurai Kusunoki Masanori who was under the employ of the emperor defected to the Ashikaga bakufu (he would later defect again to royalist forces under Emperor Kameyama in 1380). However, Kusunoki was defeated in 1390.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashikaga_Yoshimitsu#cite_note-ackroyd329-6)
While in 1370, the renowned commander Imagawa Sadayo was sent to subdue Kyushu; the region would later be pacified by 1389, which leads to Yoshimitsu distributing lands there.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashikaga_Yoshimitsu#cite_note-ackroyd329-6) There was an uprising in Kyushu but this was later suppressed in 1397 (another uprising in Mutsu was suppressed in 1402).[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashikaga_Yoshimitsu#cite_note-ackroyd330-7)
The southern army suffered reverses in 1380 but enjoyed a resurgence in 1382. The Koga Domain, a region of the Southern army was defeated in 1385.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashikaga_Yoshimitsu#cite_note-ackroyd329-6)

In 1392, the Northern and Southern courts were reconciled under Emperor Go-Komatsu.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashikaga_Yoshimitsu#cite_note-ackroyd330-7) Yoshimitsu officially ceded his position to his son Ashikaga Yoshimochi in 1394 who was appointed the new _shōgun_. The Muromachi administration was later organized in 1398.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashikaga_Yoshimitsu#cite_note-ackroyd330-7)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashikaga_Yoshimitsu#cite_note-8) Although Yoshimitsu retired in 1394, the old _shōgun_ did not abandon any of his powers. Yoshimitsu continued to maintain authority over the shogunate until his death.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashikaga_Yoshimitsu#cite_note-titsingh325-9) Yoshimitsu is recognized as _Nippon Koku-Ō_ (King of Japan) by Yongle Emperor in 1404.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashikaga_Yoshimitsu#cite_note-ackroyd330-7)
Yoshimitsu died suddenly in 1408[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashikaga_Yoshimitsu#cite_note-titsingh325-9) at age 49.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashikaga_Yoshimitsu#cite_note-10) After his death, his retirement villa (near Kyoto) became Rokuon-ji, which today is famous for its three-storied, gold-leaf covered reliquary known as "Kinkaku". So famous is this single structure, in fact, that the entire temple itself is often identified as the Kinkaku-ji, the Temple of the Golden Pavilion. A statue of Yoshimitsu is found there today.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashikaga_Yoshimitsu#cite_note-11)

Yoshimitsu resolved the rift between the Northern and Southern Courts in 1392, when he persuaded Go-Kameyama of the Southern Court to hand over the Imperial Regalia to Emperor Go-Komatsu of the Northern Court. Yoshimitsu's greatest political achievement was that he managed to bring about the end to constant fighting during the Nanboku-chō period. This event had the effect of firmly establishing the authority of the Muromachi shogunate and suppressing the power of the regional _daimyōs_ who might challenge central authority.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashikaga_Yoshimitsu#cite_note-12)
Lost statue of Ashikaga Yoshimitsu at Kinkaku-ji.
Yoshimitsu commissions the Muromachi palace in Kyoto's elite district of Kamigyo in 1378, on the site of the former residence of the nobleman Saionji Sanekane.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashikaga_Yoshimitsu#cite_note-a555-13)
He also played a major role in the genesis of Noh theatre, as the patron and lover of Zeami Motokiyo, the actor considered to be Noh's founder, whom Yoshimitsu encouraged to give a loftier treatment to his art.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashikaga_Yoshimitsu#cite_note-14)
The Ashikaga shogunate and the corresponding time period are often referred to as the Muromachi shogunate or the Muromachi period in Japanese historiography because Yoshimitsu constructed his residential headquarters along the Muromachi Road in the northern part of Kyoto in 1378.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashikaga_Yoshimitsu#cite_note-15)

## Tributary relations with the Ming dynasty
[edit]
Yoshimitsu accepted tributary relations with Ming China in 1401. In 1402 or 1404, Yoshimitsu accepted the title "King of Japan" from the Ming while the nominal sovereign of Japan still resided in Kyōto. Yoshimitsu bowed three times while kneeling and read a Ming government document addressing him as the "king of Japan" and instructing him to adopt the Ming calendar. In 1403, Yoshimitsu sent a letter to the Ming emperor addressing himself as "Your subject, the King of Japan". Yoshimitsu was the first and only Japanese leader in the early modern period to accept a title from China.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashikaga_Yoshimitsu#cite_note-16)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashikaga_Yoshimitsu#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee201719,_79-80-17) Concordant with increased communication between the Muromachi Shogunate and the Ming dynasty between 1373–1406, during this period Japan received a significant influx of Ming influence to its economic system, architecture, philosophy and religion, and writing.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashikaga_Yoshimitsu#cite_note-18)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashikaga_Yoshimitsu#cite_note-ackroyd329-6)

## Tributary relations with the Ming dynasty
The act of submission towards the Ming is viewed negatively by many modern Japanese historians. Tsuji Zennosuke and Kuroita Katsumi described Yoshimitsu's decision as a violation of Japan's national tradition, an act of disloyalty to the Japanese throne, and brought shame and disgrace to Japan. Zuikei Shuho, a contemporary of Yoshimitsu, pointed out that the word "your subject" should only be used to show allegiance to the Japanese emperor. In 1411, Yoshimitsu's successor and son, Ashikaga Yoshimochi, ended Japanese embassies to the Ming and repudiated his predecessor by stating that "ever since antiquity our country has never called itself a vassal of a foreign land".[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashikaga_Yoshimitsu#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee201793-19)
However, there were also supporters of Yoshimitsu's choice to accept official tributary status with the Ming. Arai Hakuseki, a supporter of the military class, wrote in his _Tokushi yoron_ that Yoshimitsu increased his reputation outside Japan by being recognized as the ruler of Japan by the Ming. Haruseki believed that it was proper to use the title "King of Japan" because the _shōgun_ was the de facto ruler rather than the Japanese emperor.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashikaga_Yoshimitsu#cite_note-FOOTNOTENg2019173-20)
Several explanations have been given for why Yoshimitsu accepted tributary relations with the Ming, including: he was not aware of the political significance of his action, he accepted tributary relations to increase trade, he accepted tributary relations to solidify his own position within Japan as its ruler rather than the Japanese emperor.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashikaga_Yoshimitsu#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee201793-95-21)

Due to the extraordinary achievement and similar styles of arts in Yongle and Xuande Periods, the two stages are combined and considered together by later generations. However, in terms of politics, society and economy, the reign of Emperor Yongle (1403-1424) is undoubtedly the more glorious, when the frontline during campaign against the Manchu was advanced to the estuary of Amur River. The unique military accomplishment of Emperor Yongle also included the annexion of Vietnam, winning in Mobei five times, and sending the fleet to westward voyage. His decisions on compilation of The Yongle Canon , the authorization of Neo-Confucianism as the orthodoxy and the transfer of capital city to Beijing are all extraordinary.
These influential moves embody the distinct expansionism during Yongle Period, especially on political pursuit. Apparently, Zhu Di (Emperor Yongle) was not satisfied in being the faithful successor of his father Emperor Hongwu. Instead, he wanted to be the second Kublai Khan, a UNIVERSAL RULER and an emperor beyond certain culture and ethnic group.
Emperor Yongle realized his grandiose ambition to a great extent. According to "History of Ming Dynasty, Biographic Sketch of Emperor Yongle," approximately thirty countries were under the control of Ming. The territory far exceeded the size under Han and Tang dynasties. However, the stage of expansion ended with the death of Emperor Yongle. His successor, Emperor Xuande restored Taizu's political legacy and the national policy was resumed as a decline of the country. During this period, culture and art were prosperous.
This special exhibition will display fifteen historical relics, all collections of Long Museum, including one Thangka, four buddha figures, nine porcelain pieces and one set of handwriting of the Buddhist Sutra by Zheng He. The aim is to briefly give a sample of the imperial magnificence Yongle and Xuande Periods through these few splendid relics.

While in 1370, the renowned commander Imagawa Sadayo was sent to subdue Kyushu; the region would later be pacified by 1389, which leads to Yoshimitsu distributing lands there.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashikaga_Yoshimitsu#cite_note-ackroyd329-6) There was an uprising in Kyushu but this was later suppressed in 1397 (another uprising in Mutsu was suppressed in 1402).[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashikaga_Yoshimitsu#cite_note-ackroyd330-7)
The southern army suffered reverses in 1380 but enjoyed a resurgence in 1382. The Koga Domain, a region of the Southern army was defeated in 1385.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashikaga_Yoshimitsu#cite_note-ackroyd329-6)
texts.3:
In 1392, the Northern and Southern courts were reconciled under Emperor Go-Komatsu.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashikaga_Yoshimitsu#cite_note-ackroyd330-7) Yoshimitsu officially ceded his position to his son Ashikaga Yoshimochi in 1394 who was appointed the new _shōgun_. The Muromachi administration was later organized in 1398.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashikaga_Yoshimitsu#cite_note-ackroyd330-7)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashikaga_Yoshimitsu#cite_note-8) Although Yoshimitsu retired in 1394, the old _shōgun_ did not abandon any of his powers. Yoshimitsu continued to maintain authority over the shogunate until his death.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashikaga_Yoshimitsu#cite_note-titsingh325-9) Yoshimitsu is recognized as _Nippon Koku-Ō_ (King of Japan) by Yongle Emperor in 1404.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashikaga_Yoshimitsu#cite_note-ackroyd330-7)
Yoshimitsu died suddenly in 1408[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashikaga_Yoshimitsu#cite_note-titsingh325-9) at age 49.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashikaga_Yoshimitsu#cite_note-10) After his death, his retirement villa (near Kyoto) became Rokuon-ji, which today is famous for its three-storied, gold-leaf covered reliquary known as "Kinkaku". So famous is this single structure, in fact, that the entire temple itself is often identified as the Kinkaku-ji, the Temple of the Golden Pavilion. A statue of Yoshimitsu is found there today.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashikaga_Yoshimitsu#cite_note-11)
texts.4:
Yoshimitsu resolved the rift between the Northern and Southern Courts in 1392, when he persuaded Go-Kameyama of the Southern Court to hand over the Imperial Regalia to Emperor Go-Komatsu of the Northern Court. Yoshimitsu's greatest political achievement was that he managed to bring about the end to constant fighting during the Nanboku-chō period. This event had the effect of firmly establishing the authority of the Muromachi shogunate and suppressing the power of the regional _daimyōs_ who might challenge central authority.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashikaga_Yoshimitsu#cite_note-12)
Lost statue of Ashikaga Yoshimitsu at Kinkaku-ji.
Yoshimitsu commissions the Muromachi palace in Kyoto's elite district of Kamigyo in 1378, on the site of the former residence of the nobleman Saionji Sanekane.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashikaga_Yoshimitsu#cite_note-a555-13)
He also played a major role in the genesis of Noh theatre, as the patron and lover of Zeami Motokiyo, the actor considered to be Noh's founder, whom Yoshimitsu encouraged to give a loftier treatment to his art.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashikaga_Yoshimitsu#cite_note-14)
The Ashikaga shogunate and the corresponding time period are often referred to as the Muromachi shogunate or the Muromachi period in Japanese historiography because Yoshimitsu constructed his residential headquarters along the Muromachi Road in the northern part of Kyoto in 1378.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashikaga_Yoshimitsu#cite_note-15)
texts.5:
## Tributary relations with the Ming dynasty
[edit]
Yoshimitsu accepted tributary relations with Ming China in 1401. In 1402 or 1404, Yoshimitsu accepted the title "King of Japan" from the Ming while the nominal sovereign of Japan still resided in Kyōto. Yoshimitsu bowed three times while kneeling and read a Ming government document addressing him as the "king of Japan" and instructing him to adopt the Ming calendar. In 1403, Yoshimitsu sent a letter to the Ming emperor addressing himself as "Your subject, the King of Japan". Yoshimitsu was the first and only Japanese leader in the early modern period to accept a title from China.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashikaga_Yoshimitsu#cite_note-16)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashikaga_Yoshimitsu#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee201719,_79-80-17) Concordant with increased communication between the Muromachi Shogunate and the Ming dynasty between 1373–1406, during this period Japan received a significant influx of Ming influence to its economic system, architecture, philosophy and religion, and writing.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashikaga_Yoshimitsu#cite_note-18)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashikaga_Yoshimitsu#cite_note-ackroyd329-6)
texts.6:
## Tributary relations with the Ming dynasty
The act of submission towards the Ming is viewed negatively by many modern Japanese historians. Tsuji Zennosuke and Kuroita Katsumi described Yoshimitsu's decision as a violation of Japan's national tradition, an act of disloyalty to the Japanese throne, and brought shame and disgrace to Japan. Zuikei Shuho, a contemporary of Yoshimitsu, pointed out that the word "your subject" should only be used to show allegiance to the Japanese emperor. In 1411, Yoshimitsu's successor and son, Ashikaga Yoshimochi, ended Japanese embassies to the Ming and repudiated his predecessor by stating that "ever since antiquity our country has never called itself a vassal of a foreign land".[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashikaga_Yoshimitsu#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee201793-19)
However, there were also supporters of Yoshimitsu's choice to accept official tributary status with the Ming. Arai Hakuseki, a supporter of the military class, wrote in his _Tokushi yoron_ that Yoshimitsu increased his reputation outside Japan by being recognized as the ruler of Japan by the Ming. Haruseki believed that it was proper to use the title "King of Japan" because the _shōgun_ was the de facto ruler rather than the Japanese emperor.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashikaga_Yoshimitsu#cite_note-FOOTNOTENg2019173-20)
Several explanations have been given for why Yoshimitsu accepted tributary relations with the Ming, including: he was not aware of the political significance of his action, he accepted tributary relations to increase trade, he accepted tributary relations to solidify his own position within Japan as its ruler rather than the Japanese emperor.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashikaga_Yoshimitsu#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee201793-95-21)

ASHIKAGA YOSHIMITSU (September 25, 1358 — May 31, 1408) was the third shogun of the Ashikaga shogunate and ruled Japan during the Muromachi period from 1368 to 1394. He became shogun at the age of ten and gradually strengthened his authority within both the military government and the imperial court system.
One of his main achievements was ending the division between the Northern and Southern Imperial Courts in 1392, a conflict that had lasted for more than fifty years. After this reunification, Yoshimitsu received the highest office at the imperial court — Daijō-daijin (Grand Chancellor).
In 1394, he transferred the title of shogun to his son, Ashikaga Yoshimochi, but he continued to effectively control the government. After stepping down from official power, he lived at the Kitayama-dono residence near Kyoto. It was there that the famous Golden Pavilion (Kinkaku) was built, which later became part of the Rokuon-ji temple.

Due to the extraordinary achievement and similar styles of arts in Yongle and Xuande Periods, the two stages are combined and considered together by later generations. However, in terms of politics, society and economy, the reign of Emperor Yongle (1403-1424) is undoubtedly the more glorious, when the frontline during campaign against the Manchu was advanced to the estuary of Amur River. The unique military accomplishment of Emperor Yongle also included the annexion of Vietnam, winning in Mobei five times, and sending the fleet to westward voyage. His decisions on compilation of The Yongle Canon , the authorization of Neo-Confucianism as the orthodoxy and the transfer of capital city to Beijing are all extraordinary.
These influential moves embody the distinct expansionism during Yongle Period, especially on political pursuit. Apparently, Zhu Di (Emperor Yongle) was not satisfied in being the faithful successor of his father Emperor Hongwu. Instead, he wanted to be the second Kublai Khan, a UNIVERSAL RULER and an emperor beyond certain culture and ethnic group.
Emperor Yongle realized his grandiose ambition to a great extent. According to "History of Ming Dynasty, Biographic Sketch of Emperor Yongle," approximately thirty countries were under the control of Ming. The territory far exceeded the size under Han and Tang dynasties. However, the stage of expansion ended with the death of Emperor Yongle. His successor, Emperor Xuande restored Taizu's political legacy and the national policy was resumed as a decline of the country. During this period, culture and art were prosperous.
This special exhibition will display fifteen historical relics, all collections of Long Museum, including one Thangka, four buddha figures, nine porcelain pieces and one set of handwriting of the Buddhist Sutra by Zheng He. The aim is to briefly give a sample of the imperial magnificence Yongle and Xuande Periods through these few splendid relics.
